Poverty Wage

By: Sophia Phirippides | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Millions of South Africans are living below the upper bound poverty line of R992 per person, per month, will the looming National Minimum Wage create a relieve for the working class?

Unique Selling Point:
About 60% of South African workers are living below the breadline with a majority earning less than R5000 a month. With the incumbent bench mark of R3500 minimum wage, can South Africans afford a dignified life?

Summary:
In 2016 Cyril Ramaphosa announced a national minimum wage of 20/h for South African workers effective from 1st May 2018. On a 40hours a week it amounts to R3500 or R3900 if a worker is employed for 45hours weekly. As a representative of the governing party and now president, the introduction of the NMW has been met with criticism from opposition parties and workers unions alike.

It is a slap in the face of the workers considering the cost of living in South Africa. Unions like Numsa have coined the NMW as the “Poverty Wage” with some calling it a “slave wage”. For a lot of workers in South Africa earning R3500 will not improve their lives. However Ramaphosa argues that it is an attempt to quell the levels of inequality.


Further information:
In a country riddled with so much inequality, in December 2016 the prescribed minimum wage for petrol attendants was set at R1, 126,35 per week while for cashiers it was set at R1, 207,35. A huge discrepancy compared to the top 100 JSE listed companies whose CEOs are said to be earning at a region of R69 000, per day… yes, per day, according a report by Deloitte cited on Times Live in 2017. This begs the question, how does R3500 even come close to countering inequality? In 2016, the then CEO of Shoprite, Whittey Basson, had a take home basic salary of R49.7m and yet the minimum wage for one of his floor employees is R3500!!!

No one is saying a Deli worker should earn R49.7m but R3500 is a total disregard for the struggles of the working class. According to PACSA, 73% of the so called NMW would go to food alone for a family of four, leaving the already poor worker with very little to live a dignified life. The thought is hugely commendable from the ruling party, but is it really in the interest of the working class and does it solve the continuously widening gap of inequality in South Africa. Carte Blanche investigates.

Mr. Zwelinzima Vavi
Mr. Leslie Yuill

Press Release:



Over 50% of South African workers are living below the breadline of R992 per person, per month. Government is addressing this by implementing a new income benchmark of R3500 as a minimum wage. Experts believe it’s a step in the right direction to help alleviate poverty, but some trade unions say this will only help entrench existing conditions for low-income employees. Can the majority of South African workers really survive on this minimum wage?


Script:


Link: Poverty and inequality have long been the theme for South Africa’s working class. With the looming introduction of the National Minimum Wage as of the 1st of May this year, will this be enough for the working poor?

Protest visuals against minimum wage by Numsa

VO: Recent weeks have seen protests by the National Union of Metalworkers of South Africa against the National Minimum wage (sound up protests) Irvin Jim, General Secretary of NUMSA says they will not accept what he calls a slave wage.

Irvin Jim: With petrol now being up to about 52 cents, with the VAT being imposed to the few that have jobs who supports families, extremely, this government is basically attacking the working class, the working class is under siege here.
We see it as nothing except legislation of continuation of super exploitation of black and African labour

VO: According to STATS SA over 50% of the South African population lives below the upper bound poverty line of just over R900 per month. This needs to be addressed says Vuyokazi Futshane of Oxfam.

Vuyokazi: The world bank puts us at the most unequal society in the world, along with Haiti and Namibia and then we have got a huge proportion of income inequality.

VO: Sipho is on his way to work. He uses a bicycle to cut down his transport costs, it will be 12 hours before he cycles back home from his job as a security guard in a suburban complex. Sipho earns R19.72 per hour.

Sipho: I have 3 kids, 3 girls, I struggle a lot to support them.

My wife she is not working we stay together here, she tried to look for a job everywhere she didn't get it, that’s why I decide no go stay with the kids

VO: Sipho works a 64 hour week and manages to earn R4 900 per month on his R19.72 per hour.

He pays Rent of R1500 per month, sends R2500 to his wife and children back home, and barely survives on the remaining R900.

Sipho: If I can just make my own rice, lunch for rice and buy a juice put it in a bottle I can just rob myself as a man, we are going to winter, I have to buy winter clothes but I can’t afford it.

VO: Sipho currently earns just under the prescribed National Minimum Wage for formal workers - which is R20 per hour, or R3500 per month for a 40 hour week. Minister of Labour Mildred Oliphant says there has to be an entry point.

Mildred: When you look at the national minimum wage we are just setting a standard of saying that there should be no worker who must earn below R20 per hour except where those are exempted and about 6.6m workers will benefit from the national minimum wage

VO: Government consulted with unions, together with the business community, in order to set the parameters for the National Minimum Wage

Mildred: We had the committee of experts they were looking at the economy and at the current median wage and at the various sectors in terms of the lowest paid worker and then, in order for us to afford and also to avoid retrenchment so that’s how we ended up agreeing on a R20 per hour
Vuyokazi: While it’s not necessarily something that’s going to drastically reduce inequality and poverty overnight it’s a step in the right direction

Link: Living a dignified life on a R20 per hour salary is a difficult task, but for millions of South Africans they have to take care of a family on much less.

Vuyokazi: Over 70% of farm workers are earning less than R2600, domestic workers don't fall into the category of formal workers about 90% of them earn less than R3000 as well per month

VO: Currently informal workers will earn less than the National Minimum Wage. They will be phased in over the next two years.

Vuyokazi: Then you also go into the retail sector where over half of workers in the retail sector earn less than R3000 per month

VO: Sibongile works in the formal sector as a general assistant for a major supermarket chain. A single parent, she earns around R500 per week and still lives with her mom at the age of 28.

Sibongile: I buy groceries, I shall buy for my baby some food. I buy a big milk so that it can last. Whenever I get maybe 200 or 300 I give it to my gran because she’s the one who is staying with my baby.
VO: Oupa Sebothoma was a bottle packer at an established beverage factory. They are paid R12 per packed pallet of bottles.
Oupa: If you worked really hard you would pack about 10 pallet a day, that means is R120
One pallette is 35 to 40 minutes.You try to cover to at least have R120 so that you can have ±R1800 per Month. From that R1800 subtract R600 for transport, and then subtract R600 for rent, and then and then you have to buy groceries.

Mac: Minister this NMW, do you believe that it’ll begin addressing the issue of inequality and poverty in the country

Mildred: When you look back at how much workers were earning I think it’s going to try and deal with the challenges even if it is not a living wage

VO: But Oupa's challenges were far greater. Being one of the shop stewards he was suspended in December for complaining about low wages. On some days they could earn as little as R24.
Oupa: Each and every week the company cuts because people ask questions about what the law says. So they try to kill that by accusing people of striking.

Irvin Jim: The South African economy has not been restructured in the best interest of the people of this country who are black and white. Who are the wheels of this economy. And that’s the fundamental issue in this country, it's about changing the structure of South African economy, it's not to go for sweatshop conditions for paying workers starvation wages.

Oupa: Even the food doesn’t last. You just buy pap and cabbage all the way.

VO: Oupa could no longer afford rent and the only solution was for his wife and children to leave their shack and go and live back home with her parents.
Oupa: I asked my former colleague, to help me if I could squat with him so that I can try find a job in the meantime.

Link: The current situation of low unlivable wages continues to perpetuate the legacy of Apartheid, where families are still being forced to live apart.

Sipho: they used to cry I want to see our daddy because I have no choice I have no money what can I do

VO: According to the National Minimum Wage research Institute, the working poverty line is about R4 750 per month

Vuyokazi: That brings us back to the fact that the NMW is below that but also move out of the poverty gap you would need to have enough income to secure your basic needs and also to contribute to your social development aspects as well
VO: PACSA estimates that a basic food basket would cost over R3000. Add to that transport, school fees and other household needs, and the research on what a living wage should be varies from R6000 to R12 500 per month.

Link: For years the business community has benefited from cheap labour and historically entrenched low wages in many sectors. Can businesses afford the R20 an hour minimum wage and is it economically sustainable?

VO: Alan Mukoki CEO of South African Chamber of Commerce and Industry says the timing of the minimum wage is unfavourable.

Alan: We are facing 27% unemployment rate. We have an economy which is stuttering and the growth forecast is very very very low.so why do you want to impose a minimum wage in that type of an environment?

VO: The concern is that businesses may try to find alternative solutions in order to cut costs.

Alan: If you go to the US, you pour your own petrol at the pump, you swipe your card and you leave. You go to the UK today and in many of their supermarkets you walk in and you actually scan your own goods, use your credit card and you come out.So when you then impose a standard of minimum wage in certain industries, that's gonna spell doom for the jobs that already exist in that particular market segment.

Mildred: Business has made a commitment that there is nobody who is going to retrench a person based on the agreed NMW figures.

Alan: We were consulted as business, but in the final analysis you can consult all you like, you will then get to the argument that this amount is actually not a living wage because if the social security services are not adequate, if the schooling system is not actually free the health care issues, the electricity. And the issue at the centre of everything is whether people who have been previously disadvantaged can get a dividend from this new democracy in South Africa and unfortunately for poor people they cannot say that they can at this point in time.

VO: But the prospect of a minimum wage for some is a welcome relief
Oupa: It will make a difference Even though it's not enough, it will help a lot of people.

Irvin Jim: Workers will very soon appreciate and understand that they cannot be able to live on R20 an hour especially when you have an economy that is in a crisis
So yes we reject this national minimum wage we will also be embarking on the street to mobilise the working class to reject this R20 an hour.

Mildred: We have created a condition where we are saying on top of the the NMW workers and employers must sit on the table and negotiate for a living wage

It is a slap in the face of the workers considering the cost of living in South Africa. Unions like Numsa have coined the NMW as the “Poverty Wage” with some calling it a “slave wage”. For a lot of workers in South Africa earning R3500 will not improve their lives. However Ramaphosa argues that it is an attempt to quell the levels of inequality.
metadata.Further information: In a country riddled with so much inequality, in December 2016 the prescribed minimum wage for petrol attendants was set at R1, 126,35 per week while for cashiers it was set at R1, 207,35. A huge discrepancy compared to the top 100 JSE listed companies whose CEOs are said to be earning at a region of R69 000, per day… yes, per day, according a report by Deloitte cited on Times Live in 2017. This begs the question, how does R3500 even come close to countering inequality? In 2016, the then CEO of Shoprite, Whittey Basson, had a take home basic salary of R49.7m and yet the minimum wage for one of his floor employees is R3500!!! No one is saying a Deli worker should earn R49.7m but R3500 is a total disregard for the struggles of the working class. According to PACSA, 73% of the so called NMW would go to food alone for a family of four, leaving the already poor worker with very little to live a dignified life. The thought is hugely commendable from the ruling party, but is it really in the interest of the working class and does it solve the continuously widening gap of inequality in South Africa. Carte Blanche investigates.
